verdict.headline: Gasoline drove August inflation while underlying prices slowed, and oil fell back below $100
verdict.label: August CPI rose 0.4% month over month and 3.4% over the year, both in line, with gasoline up 3.9% and accounting for over a third of the monthly increase while core slowed to 2.4% from 2.5%; WTI fell 2.17% to $99.23 on a Hormuz shipping report, equity futures rose about 0.5% and September 16 hike odds sat near 71%
verdict.rationale_short:
August consumer prices rose 0.4% from July and 3.4% over twelve months, both in line with consensus. Gasoline rose 3.9% and accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase on its own, while core prices excluding food and energy slowed to 2.4% over the year from 2.5% in July. The energy index ran 16.3% above a year earlier against food at 2.7%. The inflation in this print is energy, and the underlying price level is still decelerating.

That input started reversing the same morning the data landed. WTI fell 2.17% to $99.23 and Brent 3.58% to $103.78 after a report that Middle East foreign ministers are working on a temporary deal with Iran to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. That is the level last night's report named as what would take the energy input out of the rates move, and it traded within nine hours. Equity futures rose about 0.5% on the S&P 500 and Dow and 0.6% on the Nasdaq 100 after four straight declines took the S&P 500 to 7,591.70.

The market nonetheless goes into Wednesday's decision pricing roughly a 71% chance of a quarter-point increase, per CME FedWatch. That pricing hardened this week on PPI's energy line rather than on core data, which leaves it exposed to the same barrel now falling.

The evidence cuts both ways and the crude pullback should not be over-read. It is an intraday price on a negotiation report, not a settle, and crude still ends the week about 9% higher. More importantly, the refined product that actually reaches consumer prices is not following: US retail diesel hit a record high this week, above the 2022 peak, with distillate stockpiles at their lowest level on record for the time of year. A Hormuz arrangement can remove a crude war premium; it does not restock distillate. On the rates side, Treasury bought $5.187 billion of the $6 billion it offered in ten- to twenty-year off-the-run paper on Thursday and the ten-year rose to 4.954% after the operation, its highest since October 2023 — a mechanical bid underneath a long end that sold anyway is evidence about demand rather than about flow.

What would change the picture: a WTI settle under $100, rather than an intraday print, is the signal, and a close under it with diesel still at a record would separate the crude premium from the product cost. On the curve, hike odds holding above 60% with the ten-year back under 4.90% would say the market treats the energy line as something the Fed offsets; both rising together says the opposite. Beneath this morning's 4.94%, 4.818% is support; above Thursday's 5.37% close on the thirty-year, 5.44% is the 2007 peak. Preliminary September consumer sentiment at 10 a.m. is the first survey taken across $100 crude, against August's 51.7 index and 4.0% year-ahead inflation expectation.
verdict.lede_short: August inflation came in as expected — 0.4% on the month, 3.4% on the year — but gasoline alone carried more than a third of the increase while core prices slowed to 2.4% from 2.5%. The energy that drove the print started reversing the same morning: WTI fell back under $100 on a report of talks over Hormuz shipping. The market still prices roughly 71% odds of a hike Wednesday, built on a barrel now moving the other way; a settle under $100, not an intraday print, is the signal.

trade_setups.asset: The curve's reaction to a print whose core slowed
trade_setups.thesis: August CPI gave the front end and the long end different instructions: headline 0.4% and 3.4% in line, gasoline carrying over a third of the monthly increase, and core decelerating to 2.4% from 2.5%. The market arrives at Wednesday's decision pricing roughly 71% odds of a hike built on PPI's energy line rather than on core data, with the FOMC in blackout through September 17 and no official able to frame the print either way.
trade_setups.entry: Hike odds holding above 60% with the ten-year back under 4.90% is one reading; both rising together is the other. 4.818% is support beneath this morning's 4.94%.
trade_setups.invalidation: The ten-year clearing 5.00% on a print whose core slowed would say the long end is pricing something other than the policy path.
trade_setups.horizon: The first hour, then into the September 15-16 decision

trade_setups.thesis: Crude broke back under $100 intraday on a report of negotiations over Hormuz shipping, reversing the level the week's rate repricing was built on. The signal last night's report named was a settle, not an intraday print, and the distinction carries weight here: US retail diesel hit a record this week with distillate stockpiles at their lowest on record for the time of year, so a crude premium that a transit arrangement can remove sits on top of a product cost it cannot restock.
trade_setups.entry: $100 on WTI is the level; the close rather than the touch is what defines it. The Iran-Oman transit route is the catalyst and carries no fixed date.
trade_setups.invalidation: A settle back above $100, or diesel holding at a record while crude falls, would say the energy input into consumer prices has not left with the barrel.
trade_setups.horizon: Today's settle, then the transit-route window

trade_setups.asset: Preliminary September consumer sentiment at 10 a.m.
trade_setups.thesis: August put the University of Michigan index at 51.7 with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.0%, down from 4.2% in July, and the long-run measure steady at 3.3% for a third month. September is the first survey taken across $100 crude and record retail diesel, which makes it the first read on whether the energy shock is reaching expectations rather than only prices.
trade_setups.entry: A year-ahead reading back toward July's 4.2% is the number that matters; the long-run 3.3% is the series a committee citing anchored expectations watches.
trade_setups.invalidation: Year-ahead expectations holding at or below 4.0% despite the crude move would support looking through the energy line rather than responding to it.
